changedBeliefs: The `parameter-encoding-and-binding` open question — whether any blob-heavy parameter shape is dominated by encoding rather than SQLite stepping — is answered for the single-row blob write path. A `Uint8List` blob param is copied three times before it reaches a database page: (1) main->writer via the VM object-graph copy inside `SendPort.send` (`runtime/vm/object_graph_copy.cc` — one copy, on the sender, landing on the shared GC heap; there is NO receive-side rebuild since Dart 2.15 isolate groups), (2) writer->native param arena in `allocateParams`, (3) arena->SQLite page in `sqlite3_step`. Copies (2) and (3) are irreducible; copy (1)'s cost is not the copy itself but its destination.

Wrapping large blob params in `TransferableTypedData` is a reproduced ~15-20% end-to-end win on 256 KB-512 KB single-row blob INSERTs (256 KB -16.4%/-22.7%, 512 KB -10.4%/-11.8% across order-flipped passes; every 256/512 KB leg candidate-faster across ~7 passes, sub-threshold controls flip sign as noise). Mechanism, each part measured separately in `blob_param_mechanism_proof.dart` / `blob_param_gc_split.dart`: BOTH routes copy the payload exactly once on the main isolate (send()'s synchronous wall scales linearly with size; fromList is one linear memcpy; materialize() is ~1 us flat = a view). The win is the copy's destination — direct sends park every in-flight blob on the shared GC heap where scavenges must evacuate it (29 GCs / 8.6 ms pause vs 20 GCs / 1.2 ms per 300 x 256 KB inserts on the real path) and every collection safepoints the whole isolate group including the writer mid-step; the wrapped buffer is malloc'd external memory the GC never traces. `fromList` does NOT neuter its source, so the public caller-keeps-its-blob contract holds.

The win is size-bounded and the bounds are mechanistic, not incidental. Below ~256 KB the direct graph copy takes its fast path (new-space alloc + one unchunked memmove, ~15% over a plain copy) while the wrap still pays malloc/finalizer/materialize bookkeeping — measured +23% at 64 KB transport. At >= 1 MB two things converge: SQLite's WAL write dominates the insert, and very large payloads allocate straight to old space, skipping the new-space churn that drives the mid-size win — so end-to-end goes neutral (never negative; the wrap still trims main-isolate blocking, hence a threshold floor with no ceiling). Large direct sends additionally abort onto `CopyTypedDataBaseWithSafepointChecks` (100 KB safepoint-polled chunks, ~2x a plain memcpy at >= 1 MB), a deliberate VM trade of copy throughput for isolate-group responsiveness. Exp 005's contrast is sharpened, not inverted: its Dart codec lost because encoding *structure* is slower than the VM's native walk; a raw blob has no structure, leaving only destination and machinery costs, which the wrap avoids.
nextSignals: The batch (`BatchRequest`) and coalesced-write (`MultiExecuteRequest`) paths still route blob params through the graph copy — exp 234 deliberately scoped to single-row `ExecuteRequest`/`QueryRequest`. Open candidate: a blob-heavy `executeBatch` workload (e.g. N rows each carrying a >=256 KB blob) to test whether wrapping per-set blobs reproduces the same transfer fraction. Blocked on nothing but a bounded pass; the `blob_param_write_ab.dart` harness generalizes to batch.

The 256 KB threshold is a measured floor on an Apple M1 Pro / macOS box; the crossover between wrap-overhead and graph-copy-plus-GC cost is machine- and heap-configuration-dependent. A production profile showing a different blob-size distribution (many 64-256 KB blobs, or predominantly multi-MB) would justify re-tuning `blobParamTransferThreshold` or gating it per-arch.

The main->writer hop is now GC-invisible for large blobs, but the writer->arena copy (2) and arena->page copy (3) remain. Neither is reducible through the current Dart FFI surface (the arena must own stable native bytes for SQLITE_STATIC across the bind+step, and SQLite owns its pages), so future blob-param work should target transfer/scheduling, not copy elimination, unless a zero-copy Dart->native pin primitive ships. The Dart shared-memory multithreading proposal (dart-lang/language #333) would dissolve the isolate-hop copy entirely; it is the same watch-condition already tracked for `result-transfer-shape`.
